subcategory: California native coastal sage scrub shrub

planting.note: Direct sow in fall onto lean, well-drained slopes or plant container stock at the start of the rainy season in full sun; California sagebrush is the aromatic, finely dissected gray-green shrub that gives coastal sage scrub its name and its characteristic herbal scent, and it establishes fastest with winter rain rather than summer irrigation.

directions: Plant in lean, fast-draining soil in full sun along coastal bluffs, dry slopes, or informal borders where its soft, threadlike silvery-green foliage can be appreciated up close; the plant is grown for foliage texture and fragrance rather than its small, inconspicuous wind-pollinated flower heads produced in late summer and fall. It is a foundational shrub of coastal sage scrub, sharing habitat with black sage and California buckwheat, and provides dense cover for wrens, towhees, and other scrub-dependent birds. Once established it needs no summer water and resents heavy or frequently irrigated soils, making it a reliable low-maintenance filler for dry, exposed sites.

planting.note: Sow seed or plant container stock in fall in lean, rocky, sharply drained soil in full sun on an open slope or bank; this is the largest-growing California buckwheat and needs room to form its full mounded shape without crowding.

directions: Plant in full sun in lean, rocky or sandy, very well-drained soil; St. Catherine's lace is endemic to Santa Catalina Island and has become a popular mainland garden shrub for its enormous, felted, silver-gray leaves and towering flat-topped flowerheads, which open creamy white in late spring and age through pink to rust-brown by fall, remaining decorative as dried seed heads through winter. The huge bloom umbels are a magnet for native bees, beneficial wasps, and butterflies over an unusually long flowering season. It tolerates poor, rocky soil and needs no supplemental water once established, but will rot quickly in heavy clay or with regular irrigation.

subcategory: California native coastal sage scrub/chaparral shrub

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in fall in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; bush mallow is a fast, somewhat short-lived colonizer of disturbed slopes and recently burned chaparral, so give it an open spot where its loose, suckering habit is an asset rather than a problem.

directions: Plant in full sun in lean, fast-draining soil on an open bank or in a naturalistic native border; chaparral bush mallow is a fire-follower that resprouts vigorously from root crowns and rhizomes after burns, quickly covering bare slopes with gray-felted, maple-shaped leaves on arching canes. From spring into summer it produces a long succession of pale pink to lavender, hibiscus-like flowers that draw native bees and occasionally hummingbirds. It grows fast but can become leggy and open with age, so many gardeners cut it back hard every few years to renew dense growth; it is an easy, drought-tolerant choice for erosion control on disturbed ground.

subcategory: Channel Islands native evergreen tree/large shrub

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, giving it room to grow as a single-trunk tree or space plants closer together to form a dense evergreen hedge or screen.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Catalina cherry is the island endemic subspecies of California's native cherry, found naturally only on Santa Catalina, Santa Cruz, Santa Rosa, and San Clemente islands, where it grows as a large, dense, glossy-leaved tree far bigger than the mainland holly-leaved cherry. Clusters of small white flowers in spring give way to dark purple-black, thin-fleshed cherries in late summer that are edible in small amounts (the pit contains cyanogenic compounds and should not be eaten) and are heavily used by birds and other wildlife. Its tolerance of some shade and light coastal fog, combined with dense, wind- and salt-resistant foliage, makes it one of the best native choices for an evergreen privacy hedge or background tree in coastal Southern California gardens.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in fall as a specimen or canyon-garden tree in full sun to partial shade with good drainage; stake young trees loosely, since the shredding reddish bark and narrow canopy benefit from some wind protection while establishing.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, ideally in a sheltered canyon-style setting that mimics its native moist island ravines; Catalina ironwood is a relict species found wild only on Santa Catalina, Santa Rosa, and San Clemente islands, where it survives in small, isolated canyon groves as a living remnant of a much wider Miocene-era flora. Its shredding, cinnamon-red bark and either simple, toothed, holly-like leaves or deeply divided, fern-like leaves (in the naturally occurring fernleaf form, subspecies asplenifolius) give it striking year-round texture, and flat clusters of small, creamy-white flowers cover the canopy in early summer. It appreciates more consistent moisture during establishment than most coastal sage scrub natives, but becomes reasonably drought tolerant once its roots are deep, and is grown as a graceful specimen or street tree in mild coastal California gardens.

subcategory: California native chaparral/coastal sage scrub shrub

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in well-drained, lean soil in full sun to partial shade, such as a canyon slope or beneath the dappled edge of oak canopy, mimicking its natural chaparral and coastal sage scrub habitat.

directions: Plant in lean, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; summer holly is a large, evergreen chaparral shrub to small tree with stiff, spiny-toothed leaves that resemble true holly despite being a relative of manzanita in the heath family, found on dry slopes and canyons from San Diego County south to Santa Catalina Island and northern Baja California. Small, urn-shaped white to pale-pink flowers in spring are followed by its namesake feature, warty red berries that ripen in mid-to-late summer rather than the fall or winter timing typical of most chaparral shrubs, providing an unusual mid-summer food source for birds. It is slower-growing and less commonly available than manzanita, but makes a handsome, drought-tolerant screening or specimen shrub once established.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in partial shade to full coastal sun; it is one of the few California native shrubs that flowers reliably under the partial shade of trees or north-facing walls, where frost exposure is also reduced.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in partial shade (it also performs in full sun directly on the coast) as a sprawling border or slope cover, or trained against a wall; island bush snapdragon is native to the rocky sea bluffs of Santa Catalina, San Clemente, Anacapa, and Santa Barbara islands, and brings that cliff-dwelling toughness combined with an almost year-round show of bright red-orange, tubular, snapdragon-like flowers to the garden. The long bloom season makes it an outstanding, reliable hummingbird plant in mild coastal and near-coastal gardens. Being of island origin it is somewhat more tender to hard frost than many mainland coastal sage scrub natives, so it is best given some overhead protection or a warm microclimate in colder inland gardens.

planting.note: Sow fresh acorns directly where the tree is to grow in fall, since like other oaks it develops a long taproot early and resents transplanting; young trees appreciate light shade or wind shelter before they form their mature canopy.

directions: Plant acorns or young container trees in well-drained soil in full sun once established, siting them with room to develop a broad, rounded crown; island oak is endemic to the California Channel Islands, where it grows in moist, fog-fed canyons on Santa Cruz, Santa Rosa, San Miguel, Santa Catalina, San Clemente, and Guadalupe islands, often alongside island ironwood. Its thick, strongly veined, toothed leaves are covered beneath in a dense gray-white felt, giving the canopy a distinctive two-toned shimmer in coastal breezes, and small, slender acorns follow inconspicuous spring catkins. Historic overgrazing by feral goats and sheep on several islands reduced wild populations severely, but the species has become a valued and increasingly available slow-growing specimen tree for native gardens able to give it decades to reach full size.
